d5e34ba54f56b89718b2c6e849407bb3dedf3f8d.summary: Dutch national police (Politie) news item, published 13 November 2025, reporting that Operation Endgame disrupted the infostealer Rhadamanthys, the remote access trojan VenomRAT and the Elysium botnet. The police say these malware types infected hundreds of thousands of victims worldwide. They describe Operation Endgame as started in 2022 and as the largest international operation against ransomware and cybercrime.

d575a6482d9b8e691b7033592928e91ae53c2aa1.summary: InQuest's blog describes a holiday-season Dridex campaign that delivers malware through password-protected Microsoft Excel spreadsheets with macros. Lures included a CDC COVID-19 form, a fake resume, fake spreadsheets, and emails posing as office memos and vaccination rules that carried the spreadsheet passwords. Once opened, the macro calls an embedded script that fetches further payloads, which are distributed via Discord CDN servers. The report withholds payload URI patterns and expects Dridex to become more elusive over time.

d550bcfc9e48736defc43baa88cd510cd28b1aba.summary: FortiGuard Labs describes C0XMO, a new Gafgyt-derived botnet variant for Linux and IoT devices. It spreads by exploiting CVE-2021-27137 in the UPnP service of DD-WRT router firmware. A separate Python scanner brute-forces Telnet and SSH logins and runs HTTP exploits, including CVE-2015-2051, CVE-2022-35914, and CVE-2025-34054, to deploy bots. The malware sets up persistence with cron jobs and shell profiles, removes rival botnets, and supports 19 DDoS attack methods. The report says its design suggests more operational sophistication than typical Gafgyt malware.

d59a1a8783091b8f95332db5b53c0260c5df5a69.summary: Malpedia family page for Ryuk, a ransomware that encrypts victims' files and demands bitcoin for their release. Its only descriptive content is a short overview, including a note that Ryuk and Hermes ransomware share pieces of code. The rest is an index of third-party articles and reports about Ryuk and related groups, listed by date and source, with no analysis of its own. Classified as not a threat report.

The page says it can be delivered by spear-phishing, malvertising, exploit kits and other techniques. It lists many vendor and researcher reports from 2019 to 2026 that mention AsyncRAT, often alongside other RATs and stealers. Group names in those report titles include TAG-144, APT-C-36, TA2541, TA558, Earth Berberoka, NullBulge, MirrorFace and Transparent Tribe.

d598c8d247c607deb7db2e3ab72f2d22124f604c.summary: Article reporting a US-CERT write-up on Hoplight, a nine-file spyware kit used by the Lazarus Group (also called Hidden Cobra), which the article says is thought to be controlled by the North Korean government. Seven of the files are proxy layers that generate fake TLS handshakes, and the final file uses a certificate said to be from Naver to connect to a control server and upload pilfered files. The article says the group typically uses spear-phishing and notes its credited 2014 attack on Sony Pictures. US-CERT recommends routine patching and up-to-date malware protection.

hedges: It is not 100% clear whether the Go network tool is a system administration tool or part of the APT41 toolset.
The Go tool's purpose may not be legitimate and it may be a covert tool for destructive attacks.
The authors believe the Cloud Snooper toolset may have been in development since at least 2016.
The Two-Sail Junk name is provisional until the campaign can be linked to a known group.
The WellMess links to CozyDuke (APT29) and the healthcare focus were rumours the authors could not verify.
The Dukes is thought to be behind the 2016 Democratic National Congress hack.
Turla may have been repurposing Penguin for operations other than intelligence gathering.
The authors found no analogous later-stage Equation implants, though their existence would be suggested.
